items.def: Broadcast Hash Join: the small side is copied to every executor, so the big side does not shuffle.

Broadcast Nested Loop Join: the fallback for non-equi joins. One side is broadcast and every row pair is compared.

blocks.title: The one-sentence mental model
blocks.text: **Spark computes. Storage persists. Delta gives stored files table semantics. Unity Catalog governs the objects.** Databricks integrates these pieces into one platform.

blocks.label: Think first: why learn storage, tables and transactions before you open the Databricks UI?
blocks.text: Much of Databricks' behavior, and many exam traps, come from **mixing up layers**: compute vs storage, file vs table, Delta vs Parquet, Unity Catalog vs Delta. If you can keep these layers apart, the UI and APIs make sense.

sections.title: Compute vs Storage: Independent Lifetimes
sections.hook: Clusters come and go. Your data must not.

blocks.text: Imagine an e-shop with `customers`, `orders` and `products`. Something must **store** those bytes while nobody is processing them.
Something else must **execute** a query over them:

Amazon S3, Azure Data Lake Storage (ADLS), Google Cloud Storage (GCS)
Persistent: survives when nothing is running

items.title: Compute
points: Answers: *Which CPUs and RAM execute my code?*
For Spark: a driver plus executors

blocks.title: Independent lifetimes
blocks.text: The compute resources can disappear afterward. **The data remains.** This separation is central to modern lakehouse systems.
Why is this useful? Take a **10 TB** dataset with a compute pattern that changes every day:
You do not want your 10 TB to vanish because Tuesday has zero workers. You pay for compute only when you need it and **scale it independently** of the data.
Databricks makes the same split. The **workspace** holds artifacts and configurations, such as notebooks and settings. **Persistent data** usually lives in your cloud storage.

head: What
After you terminate the cluster
rows: Normally gone with the compute environment

blocks.title: Kitchen analogy
blocks.text: Storage is the **pantry**. Compute is the **cooks**. Send all the cooks home and the food is still in the pantry. Hire 100 cooks tomorrow and they all cook from the same pantry.

blocks.title: Don't keep anything important in compute
blocks.text: Shuffle files, local temp files and executor memory belong to the compute environment. Treat them as **disposable**. Only data written to persistent storage survives the cluster.

blocks.label: Think first: 100 TB dataset; 50 workers at 08:00, 200 at 12:00, 0 at 18:00. Why is this a good design?
blocks.text: Persistent storage survives on its own, while compute capacity **scales with the workload**. You add workers at peak, pay nothing at 18:00, and the 100 TB is untouched the whole time.

sections.title: A File Is Not a Table
sections.hook: Three Parquet files are not yet an `orders` table. Something has to say which files count.

blocks.text: Suppose storage contains:
Those are **files**. You may *logically* read them as "the `orders` table", but files alone do not give you full database-table behavior.
Now run an update on one e-shop order:

blocks.label: Think first: order 123 lives inside part-00001.parquet. Why can't the engine just change that one cell?
blocks.text: Columnar files are **immutable-ish**: values are grouped by column, encoded and compressed. They are not a grid of editable cells. The engine usually writes a **new file version** that contains the changed rows.

blocks.title: Not an Excel cell
blocks.text: Don't picture `UPDATE` as editing a cell in Excel. For columnar files the engine often has to **create a new file** that holds the changed rows.

part-00001.parquet  ──►  old file: NO LONGER part of table
part-00003.parquet  ──►  new file: NOW part of table
                (contains order 123 = 'cancelled')

    who records this?  ──►  metadata / transaction state
blocks.caption: After an UPDATE, someone must track which files count

blocks.title: The missing piece
blocks.text: Something must know *old file → no longer part of the table* and *new file → now part of the table*. That something is **metadata / transaction state**. In Databricks it is the Delta transaction log.

sections.title: What Parquet Gives You: Columnar Storage & Pruning
sections.hook: Read only the columns, and later only the files, that the query needs.

blocks.text: Take a small `people` table: `id | name | age | country`, with rows (1, Maria, 25, GR), (2, John, 37, US), (3, Anna, 42, DE).

items.def: A horizontal slice of rows inside a Parquet file.
The data of one column within one row group.
The smallest unit inside a column chunk. Encoding and compression are applied at this level.
Ways to store a column compactly. Similar values sit together, so they compress well.
Schema and statistics stored in the file footer.

blocks.text: Real Parquet is more sophisticated than this picture, but the picture explains why **analytical engines** like it.
This query needs `age`. It does not need `id`, `name`, `country`, `address`, `email`…

blocks.title: Column pruning
blocks.text: Columnar formats let the engine **skip irrelevant columns**. This is called **column pruning**. It reduces I/O.

blocks.caption: What you'll see in a Spark plan, even if the table has 100 columns

blocks.title: ReadSchema is not cosmetic
blocks.text: `ReadSchema: struct<age:int>` means Spark **requested only the column it needs** from storage. It is evidence that pruning happened, not a decorative line in the plan.
**Exercise 2.** The table is `sales(sale_id, customer_id, product_id, amount, country, timestamp, salesperson, comments)` and the query is:

blocks.label: Which columns are fundamentally needed from storage?
blocks.text: Only `country` and `amount`. The other six columns can potentially be pruned, which reduces I/O.

items.title: Data skipping / partition / clustering pruning
points: Reduces **which files or regions** are scanned
e.g. read only files for one date

blocks.title: Two different mechanisms (Challenge Q14)
blocks.text: A 5 TB table, and the query needs 2 columns and one date. **Column pruning** cuts the columns. **Data skipping / partition or clustering pruning** cuts the files or regions. They are different mechanisms, and later chapters cover each one in detail.

sections.title: Why Files Need Transactions: ACID
sections.hook: A reader must never see a state that the table was never in.

blocks.text: Imagine `/orders/` holds `A.parquet`, `B.parquet`, `C.parquet`. **Reader X** starts reading A, B, C.
At the same moment, **writer Y** runs an update and changes the directory to A, D, E.

time ─────────────────────────────────────────►
Reader X:  read A ....... read B ....... read C?
Writer Y:        [ replace B,C with D,E ]

OK      : A B C   (old state)
OK      : A D E   (new state)
DANGER  : A B E   (a state that never existed)
blocks.caption: Concurrent reader and writer on a plain directory

blocks.label: Think first: what's wrong with seeing A B E?
blocks.text: A B E may correspond to **no valid state of the table at all**: half old, half new. This is where database transactional semantics come in.

head: Letter
Meaning
E-shop example
rows: A transaction happens completely or not at all. The commit becomes visible as **one logical change**.
A pipeline replaces 80 files. Nobody should see 37 old + 43 new.
Each transaction moves the database from one valid state to another and respects enforced invariants.
An order table never ends up violating its enforced rules.
Concurrent operations don't produce invalid interleavings. A reader sees a coherent snapshot.
Reader R sees version 87 while W creates 88, never half-87-half-88.
Once a transaction commits, that state survives later process or compute failures.
The cluster crashes after the commit and the new orders are still there.

blocks.title: Two meanings of "consistency"
blocks.text: ACID **Consistency** means valid state → valid state, respecting invariants. It is **not** the C in the CAP theorem from distributed systems. Same English word, different concept.

Reader R ──► snapshot v87  (coherent)
Writer W ──► creating v88

never: rows from v87 + rows from v88 mixed
blocks.caption: Isolation

blocks.title: Why Parquet alone can't do this (Q15)
blocks.text: Parquet describes **how data is stored in files**. By itself it gives no transaction history, no atomic commits, no coherent snapshots and no table-state management. Those are what concurrent, database-like modifications need.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when a reader sees mixed or partial data
questions: Is this a plain directory of Parquet files with no transaction log?
Am I reading the files directly by path instead of through the table's committed snapshot?
Was a writer replacing files while I was reading?
Which guarantee failed: atomicity (half-done commit visible) or isolation (interleaving)?

sections.title: Delta Lake & the Transaction Log
sections.hook: Parquet holds the rows. `_delta_log` decides which files are the table.

blocks.text: Traditional **data lakes** gave cheap, scalable storage, but they historically lacked the guarantees expected from databases. Databricks' core answer is **Delta Lake**.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.text: Delta Lake extends **Parquet data files** with a **file-based transaction log**. That gives ACID transactions and scalable metadata management while staying compatible with the Spark APIs. Delta is the **default table format** on Databricks unless you specify otherwise.

my_table/
 ├─ part-00000.parquet
 ├─ part-00001.parquet
 ├─ part-00002.parquet
 └─ _delta_log/
      └─ …  (one commit per table version)
blocks.caption: A Delta table on storage (simplified)

head: Piece
Role
rows: which files make up each valid table version

blocks.text: Each version is a commit made of **ADD** and **REMOVE** actions. Replay them in order to get a snapshot:

blocks.code:
version 0:  add A   add B
version 1:  remove B   add C
version 2:  add D

snapshot(v0) = A + B
snapshot(v1) = A + C
snapshot(v2) = A + C + D
blocks.caption: Replaying the log

blocks.text: Notice that `B.parquet` may still **physically exist** for some time. The current snapshot simply says *B is not part of the current table*.

blocks.title: The essential insight
blocks.text: **Physical existence of a file ≠ logical membership in the current table.** The relevant snapshot decides membership, not the file listing.
Every topic above depends on that insight. You will meet each of them in later chapters.

blocks.title: Parquet files ≠ Delta table
blocks.text: `part-0000.parquet`, `part-0001.parquet`… do **not** automatically mean you have a Delta table. Without a `_delta_log` there is no transaction log, so it is not Delta.

blocks.title: Uncommitted files are invisible (Q11)
blocks.text: If Spark has physically written three replacement files but the transaction has **not committed**, readers of the current table must not see them. Creating files is not the same as **publishing a committed version**.

blocks.title: Read the table, not the folder
blocks.text: If you list the folder, or read it as plain Parquet, you see **every** physical file, including removed and uncommitted ones. Read through the Delta table so that the log decides what counts.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when files exist in storage but their rows aren't in the table
questions: Does the current snapshot reference this file, or did a later version REMOVE it?
Did the transaction that wrote this file ever commit?
Was this file dropped into the folder by a plain Parquet write that never touched the log?
Am I treating physical existence as logical membership?

sections.title: SQL Operations vs Physical Files
sections.hook: `DELETE` looks like row surgery. Underneath, it is a file swap plus a commit.

blocks.text:
A.parquet            B.parquet
──────────           ──────────
120                  120
121                  121
123   ── rewrite ──► 124
124                  125
125

commit:  REMOVE A.parquet   ADD B.parquet
before:  table → A        after:  table → B
blocks.caption: A DELETE as a file rewrite plus a transaction

blocks.text: The operation looks like normal database **DML** (`DELETE`). Underneath it may involve **file-level rewriting** and **transaction metadata**.

blocks.title: This model will get more detail
blocks.text: Modern Delta has extra mechanisms and optimizations that refine this picture in later chapters. The rewrite + REMOVE/ADD model is still the correct foundation.

blocks.title: "Deleted" ≠ physically erased
blocks.text: After the commit, `A.parquet` is no longer part of the table, but it may still **physically exist** for a while. The snapshot changed. The bytes in storage didn't have to.

blocks.label: Think first (Q3): why can a Delta DELETE create new Parquet files?
blocks.text: Columnar data files are not edited as individual mutable cells. A change may produce **replacement files**, plus transaction metadata recording which files now belong to the table.

blocks.caption: The lakehouse idea, roughly

blocks.text: **Delta Lake** is a major part of how Databricks gives object-storage data database-like table semantics. Databricks describes Delta as the **optimized storage layer underpinning lakehouse tables**.

blocks.title: Not "Spark with notebooks"
blocks.text: Databricks is **not** simply Spark with notebooks. The platform connects storage, transactional tables, Spark/Photon compute, governance, orchestration, SQL/BI, ML/AI and DevOps.

blocks.title: Q13: Is Delta Lake a database?
blocks.text: "Delta Lake is a database" is imprecise. Delta Lake is a **transactional storage/table layer over files**, not a standalone traditional database server.

blocks.label: Think first: what does the lake bring, and what does the warehouse bring?
blocks.text: The lake brings cheap object storage, files, flexible formats and room for raw/ML data. The warehouse brings tables, SQL, transactions, governance and BI performance. The lakehouse aims to combine both on the same data.

sections.title: Table Metadata & the Unity Catalog Namespace
sections.hook: How does `prod.sales.orders` turn into actual files? Through metadata.

blocks.text: How does the system know what `prod.sales.orders` means? It needs **metadata**.

blocks.title: Metadata ≠ data
blocks.text: **Metadata describes the data.** Keep these apart and Unity Catalog becomes easy to understand later.
In modern Databricks, **Unity Catalog** organizes governed objects with a **three-level namespace**, and it is the centralized governance layer for tables and other data/AI assets.

SELECT * FROM ecommerce.silver.orders;

ecommerce  ◄ catalog
silver     ◄ schema
orders     ◄ table (object)
blocks.caption: Reading a three-level name

blocks.title: Not server.database.table
blocks.text: Don't map `catalog.schema.object` onto `server.database.table` from traditional databases. The first part is a **catalog**, not a server. Exact semantics come later.

blocks.title: Unity Catalog ≠ Delta Lake
blocks.text: Unity Catalog = **metadata + governance** (names, ownership, permissions). Delta Lake = **transactional table format** over files. They work together but are different layers.

blocks.label: Think first: in `company.finance.transactions`, which part is the catalog?
blocks.text: `company` is the catalog, `finance` is the schema and `transactions` is the object (table).

blocks.text: You already know `spark.read.parquet(...)` and `df.write.parquet(...)`. **Spark** is the processing engine. **Parquet** is a storage file format.

blocks.code:
df = spark.read.parquet(path)          # Spark reads Parquet files
df.write.parquet(path)                  # Spark writes Parquet files

df.write.format("delta").save(path)    # Parquet files + Delta log
df.write.saveAsTable("catalog.schema.orders")  # governed table

blocks.text:
Unity Catalog object   (catalog.schema.orders)
        │
        ▼
   Delta table
        │
        ▼
  cloud storage
blocks.caption: saveAsTable adds a governed layer

blocks.title: Don't memorize syntax yet
blocks.text: Later chapters take each form apart, including when these snippets are equivalent and when they **absolutely are not**.
**Databricks-style question:** you run `df.write.saveAsTable("prod.sales.orders")`, then later terminate the compute resource. Does `prod.sales.orders` necessarily disappear?

blocks.title: Cluster gone ≠ table gone
blocks.text: **No.** The compute environment and the persistent data have **different lifetimes**. This sounds trivial, but it explains a large class of Databricks architecture questions.

blocks.title: Spark vs Delta (Q2)
blocks.text: Spark is mainly a **distributed computation engine**. Delta Lake supplies **transactional table/storage semantics** over data files.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when a table "disappeared" after the cluster was terminated
questions: Am I confusing the compute resource (driver, executors, RAM) with the table (files + log in cloud storage)?
Was the data ever persisted with `saveAsTable` or `format("delta").save`, or did it only live in a DataFrame in memory?
Did the write actually commit a table version?
Am I querying the exact `catalog.schema.table` name I wrote to?

sections.title: Control Plane vs Compute Plane (Preview)
sections.hook: One side decides what should run. The other side runs it.

items.title: Compute plane
points: Where your workload actually processes data
Classic: cloud infrastructure in the **customer's** cloud environment

blocks.text:
CONTROL PLANE  (Databricks-managed services, web app)
      │  "What should run?"
      ▼
COMPUTE PLANE  (where data is processed)
   ├─ serverless → Databricks-managed serverless plane
   └─ classic    → customer's cloud environment
      "Actually run it."
blocks.caption: First preview. Later chapters make it precise

blocks.title: Where does compute live?
blocks.text: **Serverless** workloads run on compute that Databricks operates in a **Databricks-managed serverless compute plane**. **Classic** compute uses cloud infrastructure associated with the **customer's** cloud environment.

blocks.title: Restaurant analogy
blocks.text: The control plane is the **front office**: it takes orders and coordinates. The compute plane is the **kitchen** where the cooking happens. With serverless, the restaurant also runs the kitchen. With classic compute, the kitchen sits in your building.

blocks.label: Think first: where does the Databricks web UI belong?
blocks.text: In the **control plane**, which holds the Databricks-managed backend services, including the web application and platform coordination.

sections.title: Debugging Mindset & Round-1 Review
sections.hook: "Spark is slow" isn't a diagnosis. Find the layer first.

blocks.caption: It's extremely slow. Which layer is responsible?

blocks.text: A beginner answers "Spark". That's **insufficient**: many layers could be the cause.

blocks.title: "Query slow → increase cluster size"
blocks.text: Throwing more compute at every slow query is the anti-pattern. It skips identifying the layer and collecting evidence. This is the difference between someone who **uses** Databricks and someone who can **operate** it professionally.

blocks.title: Ask yourself when a query is extremely slow
questions: Which layer could this be: storage, table layout, Delta, Spark, data, compute, query, statistics or network?
What evidence do I have, or have I only guessed?
Am I reading too many tiny files, or a badly organized table?
Is there an enormous shuffle or a huge exchange over the network?
Did the optimizer choose badly because of missing or stale statistics?
After my fix, did I remeasure?

steps.do: Restate the model: compute and persistent storage have independent lifetimes.
steps.why: Terminating compute removes RAM and temporary shuffle files, not the table.

steps.do: Query the full name from new compute.
steps.why: Rules out a wrong catalog or schema.
A DataFrame that was never written lived only in executor memory.

steps.do: Confirm the write committed (a new version exists in the table's log).
steps.why: Physically written but uncommitted files are not a published table.

rootCauses: Mental model error: equating cluster lifetime with table lifetime
Data was never persisted (only an in-memory DataFrame)
debug.fix: Query the table from any compute using its full three-level name. If it was never persisted or committed, write it with saveAsTable (or format("delta").save) and confirm the commit.

debug.title: Reader sees a partial / mixed state (e.g. A B E)
debug.symptom: A query that ran during an update returns a mix of old and new rows (or duplicates), a state the table was never in.
askYourself: Is this a plain directory of Parquet files with no transaction log (no `_delta_log/`)?
Am I reading the files directly by path, as plain Parquet, instead of through the table's committed snapshot?
Was a writer replacing files while I was reading?
Which guarantee failed: atomicity (half-finished change visible) or isolation (invalid interleaving)?
Does my reader stay on one snapshot version (e.g. 87) while the writer builds 88?

steps.do: Check the table folder for a `_delta_log/` directory.
steps.why: Without a transaction log, there are no atomic commits or snapshots.

steps.do: Check how the reader reads: table name / Delta format vs plain `spark.read.parquet(path)`.
steps.why: A plain Parquet read lists every physical file and ignores the log.

steps.do: Line up the timing of the read and the concurrent write.
steps.why: Confirms an overlap that let the reader see an in-between state.

rootCauses: Plain Parquet directory with no transactional layer
Reader bypasses the Delta log (reads files by path as Parquet)
Writer's partial progress is visible because nothing makes the commit atomic
debug.fix: Store the data as a Delta table and read it through Delta (table name or format("delta")), so every reader sees exactly one committed snapshot.
debug.mnemonic: ABE is a lie: only ABC or ADE.

debug.title: Files exist in storage, but their rows aren't in the table
debug.symptom: Listing the table folder shows `X.parquet`, but SELECT on the table never returns X's rows.
askYourself: Does the current snapshot reference X, or did a later version REMOVE it?
Did the transaction that wrote X ever commit?
Was X dropped into the folder by a plain Parquet write that never touched the log?
Am I treating physical existence as logical membership?

steps.do: Confirm the symptom by querying the table, not the folder.
steps.why: The folder listing is physical. The table is logical.

steps.do: Replay the log versions (ADD/REMOVE) up to the current one.
steps.why: Membership is defined by the snapshot.
steps.code:
v0: ADD A ADD B
v1: REMOVE A ADD C
…

steps.do: If X was never ADDed: check whether its writer failed before committing, or wrote plain Parquet.
steps.why: Uncommitted or out-of-band files are not published versions.

rootCauses: X was removed by a later commit (e.g. UPDATE/DELETE rewrite) but not yet physically cleaned up
X was written by a path that bypassed the Delta log
debug.fix: Accept that removed files are expected leftovers. For missing data, rerun the write through Delta so it commits an ADD. Never point a plain Parquet reader at the folder or touch `_delta_log` by hand.

debug.title: Query is extremely slow
askYourself: Which layer could it be: storage, table layout, Delta, Spark, data, compute, query, statistics or network?
What evidence do I actually have, or have I only guessed?
Am I reading too many tiny files or a badly organized table?
Is there an enormous shuffle or a huge exchange over the network?
Is a key (e.g. one country) severely skewed?
Are the resources insufficient, or is the transformation itself inefficient?
Did the optimizer choose badly because statistics are missing or stale?
After the fix, did I remeasure?

steps.do: Name the symptom precisely (which stage, how slow compared with normal).
steps.why: A vague symptom leads to a vague fix.

steps.do: Collect evidence and form a hypothesis.
steps.why: e.g. a scan with a huge file count → tiny files; one long task → skew.

steps.do: Apply a targeted fix and remeasure.
steps.why: Only measurement proves the fix worked.

debug.fix: Follow symptom → identify layer → collect evidence → form hypothesis → check metrics → fix → remeasure. Never default to "increase cluster size".
debug.mnemonic: Layers: "Some Tables Deliver Slow Data; Check Query Stats Now" (storage, table layout, Delta, Spark, data, compute, query, statistics, network).

pitfalls.title: UPDATE/DELETE as cell edits
pitfalls.text: Picturing UPDATE/DELETE as editing a cell in Excel.
pitfalls.fix: Columnar files get rewritten: write a replacement file, then commit REMOVE old + ADD new.

pitfalls.title: Physical existence = membership
pitfalls.text: Assuming a file in the table folder is part of the current table.
pitfalls.fix: The current snapshot (from the log) decides membership. Removed or uncommitted files can still sit in storage.

pitfalls.title: Seeing uncommitted files
pitfalls.text: Expecting readers to see files that were written but not yet committed.
pitfalls.fix: Only a committed version is published. Writing files is not committing.

pitfalls.title: ACID consistency vs CAP consistency
pitfalls.text: Treating the C in ACID as the C in CAP.
pitfalls.fix: ACID C = valid state → valid state respecting invariants. CAP C is a distributed-systems property.

pitfalls.title: Cluster terminated = table deleted
pitfalls.fix: Compute and persistent storage have independent lifetimes.

pitfalls.title: Relying on compute-local data
pitfalls.text: Expecting executor RAM or shuffle/temp files to survive the cluster.
pitfalls.fix: They are disposable. Persist important data to cloud storage as a table.

pitfalls.title: Unity Catalog = Delta Lake
pitfalls.text: Mixing up the governance layer with the table format.
pitfalls.fix: UC = metadata + governance. Delta = transactional table layer over files.

pitfalls.title: "Delta Lake is a database"
pitfalls.fix: Delta is a transactional storage/table layer over files, not a standalone database server.

pitfalls.title: Databricks = Spark with notebooks
pitfalls.text: Reducing Databricks to its compute engine.
pitfalls.fix: It connects storage, Delta tables, Spark/Photon, governance, orchestration, SQL/BI, ML/AI and DevOps.

pitfalls.title: ReadSchema is cosmetic
pitfalls.fix: It shows the columns Spark actually requests, which is evidence of column pruning.

pitfalls.title: Column pruning = file skipping
pitfalls.text: Thinking column pruning also skips files or dates.
pitfalls.fix: Column pruning cuts columns. Data skipping / partition / clustering pruning cuts files or regions.

pitfalls.title: Query slow → bigger cluster
pitfalls.fix: Symptom → identify layer → evidence → hypothesis → metrics → fix → remeasure.

pitfalls.title: Serverless vs classic location
pitfalls.text: Assuming classic compute runs in the Databricks-managed plane.
pitfalls.fix: Serverless runs in a Databricks-managed serverless compute plane. Classic runs in the customer's cloud environment.

exercises.q: Which topic is **NOT** part of *Prerequisites — Round 1* in the mastery DAG?
why: Correct: this is the first Round 2 topic.
Round 1: the core of Delta Lake.
exercises.explain: ETL vs ELT opens **Round 2**, which moves from the storage model to the pipeline model. Round 1 is about storage, tables and transactions: compute vs storage, object storage, file ≠ table, Parquet, metadata, ACID, transaction logs and the lakehouse motivation.

exercises.q: Complete the chapter mantra.
exercises.text: Spark [[computes]]. Storage [[persists]]. [[Delta|Delta Lake]] gives stored files table semantics. [[Unity Catalog|UC]] governs the objects. Databricks [[integrates]] these pieces into one platform.
exercises.explain: Each clause names one layer and its single job. Spark (compute) **computes**. Cloud storage **persists**. Delta turns stored Parquet files into **tables** with transactions. Unity Catalog **governs** (names, permissions). Databricks is the platform that **integrates** all of them.

exercises.q: Match each Spark abbreviation you already studied to its meaning.
exercises.explain: These are the four physical join strategies plus AQE from your Spark foundation. BHJ avoids shuffling the big side by broadcasting the small one. SMJ shuffles and sorts both sides. SHJ shuffles both sides and hashes per partition. BNLJ is the costly fallback for non-equi joins. AQE re-plans at runtime from real statistics.

exercises.q: The current Databricks Data Engineer Associate exam is mostly about memorizing syntax. Operational topics such as OOM diagnosis and skew are not tested.
exercises.explain: False. The current exam guide explicitly includes Spark UI troubleshooting, skew/shuffle/spill, **OOM diagnosis**, CI/CD/Automation Bundles, Lakeflow Jobs and governance. That is why this course trains reasoning and debugging, not just syntax.

exercises.q: Which of these are named in the source as topics of the current Associate exam? (Select all that apply.)
why: Not listed. JVM internals are not part of the exam.
exercises.explain: Liquid Clustering, predictive optimization, Spark UI troubleshooting and CI/CD with Automation Bundles all appear in the exam list. Writing custom JVM garbage collectors does not. The exam tests platform operation, not JVM internals.

exercises.q: Sort each topic into its place in the mastery DAG.
exercises.explain: Your **existing Spark knowledge** covers the execution engine: Catalyst, AQE, the DataFrame API and joins. **Round 1** builds the storage and table model (compute vs storage, ACID, transaction logs, lakehouse motivation). **Round 2** starts the pipeline model with ETL vs ELT.

exercises.q: Put the learning path in order.
items: Prerequisites Round 2: pipeline model (ETL vs ELT …)
exercises.explain: The path starts from the Spark engine you already know. Round 1 builds the storage model. Round 2 builds the pipeline model. Only then do you enter Databricks proper. Each stage depends on the vocabulary of the stage before it.

exercises.q: Your Spark cluster (driver, worker1, worker2, worker3) reads `s3://shop/orders/`. You **terminate the cluster**. Sort each item.

items.text: Spark shuffle files on local worker disks
Temporary local data written by Spark during a job

exercises.explain: Everything that lives in the compute environment (executor RAM, driver memory, local shuffle/temp files) disappears with it. Files in persistent object storage, such as `s3://shop/orders/` or an ADLS path, remain. This difference returns later as compute vs Delta tables.

exercises.q: Storage is the layer that answers *"Which CPUs and RAM execute my code?"*
exercises.explain: False. That question belongs to **compute** (driver and executors). Storage answers *"Where are the bytes after my program stops running?"* Keeping the two questions apart is the first step of the chapter's mental model.

exercises.q: After the cluster that ran a big `groupBy` is terminated, what normally happens to the **shuffle files** it wrote?
options: They are kept in `s3://shop/orders/` next to the data
They normally disappear with the compute environment
They are converted to Parquet and committed to the table
They are moved to the control plane for reuse
why: Shuffle files live on the workers' local disks, not in your object storage path.
Correct: they are temporary and owned by compute.
Nothing commits shuffle output to a table automatically.
The control plane runs platform services. It does not store your shuffle data.
exercises.explain: Shuffle files are temporary local data owned by the compute environment, so they normally disappear with it. They are never automatically published into the table's storage location. Only data that was explicitly written to persistent storage survives.

exercises.q: Match each address or component to what it is.
exercises.explain: `s3://` is Amazon S3, `abfss://…dfs.core.windows.net` is Azure Data Lake Storage, and `gs://` is Google Cloud Storage. All three are **persistent object storage**. An executor is different: it is CPU and RAM, so it belongs to compute.

exercises.q: A **100 TB** persistent dataset is processed by 50 workers at 08:00 and 200 workers at 12:00. At 18:00 the cluster scales to **0 workers**. How many TB of the dataset still exist in storage at 18:00?
exercises.explain: All **100 TB** remain, because storage and compute have independent lifetimes. Scaling compute to zero only stops processing and billing for workers. The trap is to think that 'no cluster' means 'no data'.

exercises.q:
**Challenge Q12.** Why is this architecture useful?
`100 TB persistent dataset` · `08:00 → 50 workers` · `12:00 → 200 workers` · `18:00 → 0 workers`
exercises.model: Because storage and compute are decoupled: the 100 TB lives in persistent object storage that survives independently, while compute can be scaled up (200 workers at peak), down, or to zero according to the workload. You pay for compute only when you need it, and terminating workers never deletes the data.
rubric: Compute scales up/down (even to zero) with workload
Terminating compute does not delete data
exercises.explain: Persistent storage survives on its own while compute capacity scales with the workload. You pay for 200 workers only at peak, for zero at night, and the data is never at risk because it does not live on the workers.

exercises.q: Which one doesn't belong?
exercises.explain: Amazon S3, ADLS and GCS are all **persistent cloud object storage**. A Spark executor is **compute**: CPUs and RAM that disappear when the cluster is terminated.

exercises.q: `UPDATE orders SET status='cancelled' WHERE order_id=123` edits the single value for order 123 directly inside the existing Parquet file, like editing a cell in Excel.
exercises.explain: False. Columnar files are not manipulated as individual mutable cells. The engine usually writes a **new file version** with the changed rows, and metadata records that the old file is out and the new file is in.

exercises.q: Fill the gaps.
exercises.text: `part-00000.parquet`, `part-00001.parquet` … are [[physical|physical files]] objects. "The `orders` table" is a [[logical]] interpretation of them. Knowing which file currently belongs to the table requires [[metadata|transaction state]].
exercises.explain: The part files are **physical** objects. "The orders table" is a **logical** interpretation of them. The link between the two, saying which files currently belong to the table, is **metadata** (transaction state).

exercises.q: The directory `/orders/` contains three `part-0000N.parquet` files. Which statement is most accurate?
options: They are a full database table with ACID guarantees
They are files you may interpret as a table, but files alone don't provide full table behavior
They are a Delta table, because Delta stores data as Parquet
They are a Unity Catalog object, because they live in cloud storage
why: Plain files have no transaction state, so there is no ACID.
Delta also needs a `_delta_log`. Parquet alone is not Delta.
Unity Catalog objects are registered metadata. Files in storage are not automatically UC objects.
exercises.explain: Files can be *interpreted* as a table, but they don't bring table behavior such as atomic updates, coherent snapshots or a record of which files belong. Those come from metadata and transaction state. Having Parquet files also does not make something a Delta table automatically.

exercises.q: A teammate wrote these notes. Click the **wrong** statements.
lines: These files automatically behave like a full database table
UPDATE rewrites only that one cell inside part-00001.parquet, in place
Something must record that the old file is out and the new file is in
exercises.fix:
Line 1 → 'These files can be interpreted as a table, but files alone don't provide full table behavior.'
Line 3 → 'UPDATE typically writes a new file with the changed rows; metadata/transaction state marks the old file as removed and the new file as added.'
exercises.explain: "These files automatically behave like a full database table" is wrong: files alone don't give table semantics. "UPDATE rewrites only that one cell … in place" is wrong: the engine writes a replacement file instead of editing cells in a columnar file. The other lines describe the correct model.

exercises.q: In 2–3 sentences, explain why a directory of Parquet files is **not** the same as a table.
exercises.model: Files are physical bytes in storage; a table is a logical object. After an UPDATE/DELETE the engine writes replacement files, so something (metadata/transaction state) must record which files currently belong to the table and which are obsolete. A bare directory has no such record, so it can't provide full table behavior.
exercises.explain: A table is a logical object with defined membership, a schema and transactional behavior. A directory is just bytes. You need metadata or transaction state to know which files make up the table at each moment, especially after updates create replacement files.

exercises.q: Which one doesn't belong?
exercises.explain: The three `part-*.parquet` items are **physical files** in storage. "The `orders` table" is a **logical** concept, and you need metadata to know which files make it up.

exercises.q: **Exercise 2.** `sales(sale_id, customer_id, product_id, amount, country, timestamp, salesperson, comments)`. Which columns does this query fundamentally need from storage? (Select all.)
exercises.explain: Only `country` (grouping key) and `amount` (aggregated value) are needed. Thanks to the columnar format, Spark can prune the other six columns and read less. `sale_id` is a tempting wrong pick, but nothing in the query references it.

exercises.q: **Challenge Q5.** Why can `SELECT AVG(age) FROM people;` read far less data from Parquet than from a row-oriented representation?
options: Parquet files are always smaller than any other format
Parquet is columnar, so Spark can prune and read only the `age` column
Parquet keeps a transaction log that indexes ages
Parquet caches the average in its footer
why: Size alone isn't the point. Being able to read only one column is.
A transaction log is a Delta feature, not a Parquet one.
Parquet stores statistics, but this answer misstates the mechanism.
exercises.explain: Parquet is **columnar**, so Spark can do column pruning and fetch only the `age` column. In a row layout every row carries all its columns together, so you read the bytes of `name`, `email` and so on just to reach `age`. Compression helps too, but the main reason is column access.

exercises.q: Fill the gaps.
exercises.text: Avoiding reading irrelevant columns is called [[column pruning]]. In the physical plan for `SELECT AVG(age) FROM people` you may see `ReadSchema: struct<[[age]]:int>` even though the table has 100 columns.
exercises.explain: Skipping irrelevant columns is **column pruning**. The physical plan shows it as `ReadSchema: struct<age:int>`: only `age` was requested even if the table has 100 columns.

exercises.q: `ReadSchema: struct<age:int>` in a plan is cosmetic. Spark still reads all 100 columns from storage.
exercises.explain: False. ReadSchema shows the columns Spark actually **requests** from the files. A single column there is evidence that column pruning reduced I/O.

exercises.q: Idealized model: a Parquet table has **100 columns of equal size**. Approximately what **percentage** of the column data does `SELECT AVG(age)` need to read thanks to column pruning?
exercises.explain: 1 of 100 equal-size columns is **1%**. Real numbers differ because columns differ in size and compression, but the order of magnitude shows why column pruning matters for wide tables.

exercises.q: A table occupies **5 TB**, stored as **50 columns of equal size**. Your query needs **2 columns**. With column pruning alone (no file skipping), roughly how many TB must be read?
exercises.explain: 2/50 × 5 TB = **0.2 TB**. Data skipping or partition/clustering pruning could cut this further by scanning only the files for the requested date. That second mechanism is separate from column pruning.

exercises.q: Sort each situation by the mechanism that reduces the read.
buckets: Data skipping / partition / clustering pruning (fewer files/regions)

items.text: Only files for one date are scanned
Files whose statistics exclude the filter value are skipped
Only one partition directory is read

exercises.explain: **Column pruning** reduces *which columns* are read and relies on the columnar format. **Data skipping / partition / clustering pruning** reduces *which files or regions* are scanned and relies on layout and statistics (such as min/max values per file). Q14 asks you to name one of each.

exercises.q: **Challenge Q14 (debugging).** A table occupies 5 TB in cloud storage, but your query needs two columns and rows from one date. Name **two fundamentally different mechanisms** that could reduce what Spark has to read.
exercises.model: 1) Column pruning: because the format is columnar, Spark reads only the two needed columns. 2) Data skipping / partition pruning / clustering-based pruning: using table layout and statistics, Spark skips files or regions that cannot contain the requested date.
rubric: Data skipping / partition / clustering pruning (fewer files/regions)
States that the two are different axes
exercises.explain: The key word is *different*. One mechanism trims the read vertically (columns) and the other trims it horizontally (files or regions). Naming two kinds of pruning that both cut columns would miss the point.

exercises.q: Write the Exercise 2 query: total `amount` per `country` from `sales`.
exercises.explain: `GROUP BY country` with `SUM(amount)` needs only those two columns. That makes it a textbook case for column pruning on a columnar format.

exercises.q: Click the wrong line(s) in this query analysis.
lines: Query: SELECT country, SUM(amount) FROM sales GROUP BY country
Columnar format lets Spark prune the other columns
Column pruning also lets Spark skip files from other dates
exercises.fix: Remove line 2: sale_id is not needed. Line 4 → 'Skipping files from other dates is data skipping / partition / clustering pruning, a different mechanism from column pruning.'
exercises.explain: "Also needed: sale_id" is wrong: `sale_id` is not referenced, so it can be pruned. "Column pruning also lets Spark skip files" is wrong: column pruning reduces columns, not files. Skipping files for a date is data skipping or partition/clustering pruning.

exercises.q: Reader X starts reading A, B, C while writer Y changes the directory to A, D, E. Which results would be **valid** for X to see? (Select all.)
why: A union of two states is not a state the table was ever in.
exercises.explain: Valid results are complete states: the old one (A B C) or the new one (A D E). Mixtures such as A B E, or a union of both like A B C D E, represent **no valid table state**. Preventing them is the job of transactional semantics.

exercises.q: Match each ACID property to its meaning.
pairs: Completely or not at all: one logical change
Valid state → valid state, respecting invariants
Concurrent ops don't interleave invalidly; coherent snapshot
Committed state survives later compute failure
exercises.explain: Atomicity is all-or-nothing visibility. Consistency is valid → valid while respecting invariants. Isolation means no invalid interleavings, so each reader gets a coherent snapshot. Durability means committed state survives failures.

exercises.q: The C in ACID means the same thing as the C (Consistency) in the CAP theorem.
exercises.explain: False. ACID consistency means a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another while respecting invariants. CAP consistency is a distributed-systems property about replicas agreeing. Same word, different concept, and a classic trap.

exercises.q: **Challenge Q6.** A reader sees some files from **before** a transaction and some files created **during** it. What's the problem, and which ACID idea is most directly involved?
options: An invalid partial state; atomic visibility / isolation
Schema mismatch; consistency in the CAP sense
why: No committed data is lost here.
This is about correctness, not speed.
CAP consistency is a different concept.
exercises.explain: The reader observes an **invalid partial state** that never existed as a committed table. Atomic visibility of commits and isolation between reader and writer are the guarantees that prevent this. Durability is about surviving crashes after the commit, so it is not the answer here.

exercises.q: Fill the gaps about isolation.
exercises.text: Reader R should see a coherent snapshot such as version [[87]] while writer W creates version [[88]], and never a half-87-half-88 dataset. This ACID property is [[isolation]].
exercises.explain: Isolation means reader R keeps a coherent snapshot (version 87) while writer W builds version 88. A dataset that is half 87 and half 88 is an invalid interleaving.

exercises.q: A pipeline replaces **80 files** atomically. Halfway through the write, 43 new files physically exist. How many of the **new** files may a concurrent reader of the current table see **before the commit**?
exercises.explain: **0.** With atomicity the change becomes visible as one logical commit, so before it a reader sees only the old state and after it only the new one. Seeing 43 new files plus 37 old ones is exactly the partial state atomicity forbids.

exercises.q: **Challenge Q15 (critical thinking).** Why isn't adding ACID semantics to an object store simply a matter of "store everything as Parquet"?
exercises.model: Parquet describes how data is stored inside files; by itself it provides no transaction history, no atomic commits, no coherent snapshots for readers, and no table-state management (which files belong to which version). Those are required for database-like concurrent modifications — which is why Delta adds a transaction log on top of Parquet.
exercises.explain: The trap is to treat a file format as a transaction system. Parquet is about layout inside a file. ACID is about state across files and over time, so it needs a log or protocol on top.

exercises.q: Which one doesn't belong?
exercises.explain: Atomicity, Isolation and Durability are ACID transaction guarantees. Column pruning is a read optimization made possible by columnar formats and has nothing to do with transactional correctness.

exercises.q: A dashboard query on `/orders/` ran while the nightly job was replacing files. It returned rows from `A`, `B` and `E`, a mix that matches neither the old nor the new state.

options.text: Whether `/orders/` is a plain Parquet directory (no `_delta_log/`) or a Delta table
options.fb: Right. Without a transaction log, nothing makes a commit atomic.

options.text: Whether the cluster had enough memory
options.fb: Memory doesn't cause a mixed table state.

options.text: Whether the query used column pruning
options.fb: Column pruning changes which columns are read, not which version is seen.

steps.prompt: It *is* a Delta table. What next?

options.text: Check whether the dashboard reads the folder as plain Parquet (`spark.read.parquet(path)`) instead of through Delta
options.fb: Correct. A plain Parquet read lists every physical file and ignores the log's snapshot.

options.text: Delete the `_delta_log` folder and retry
options.fb: Destroys the table state. Never do this.

options.text: Schedule the dashboard so it never overlaps the job
options.fb: That hides the symptom. Proper isolation makes overlap safe.

steps.prompt: Which ACID ideas does the fix restore?

options.text: Atomic visibility of commits + isolation (one coherent snapshot per reader)
options.fb: Yes. The reader sees v87 or v88, never half of each.

options.text: Durability only
options.fb: Durability is about surviving failures after a commit.

options.text: CAP consistency
options.fb: A different concept from ACID.

exercises.explain: Mixed states come from the lack of a transactional layer: no log, or a reader that bypasses it. The fix is to make commits atomic and reads snapshot-based (Delta, read through the table), not to time jobs carefully or add compute.

exercises.q: Order the checks for *"a reader saw a mixed/partial state"*.
items: Check for a `_delta_log/` (is there a transaction log?)
Check that the reader goes through the table/Delta, not plain Parquet by path
Confirm a writer was replacing files during the read
Name the violated guarantee: atomicity / isolation
exercises.explain: First establish whether a transactional layer exists at all, then whether the reader actually uses it. Then confirm the overlap with a writer, and finally name the violated guarantee so the fix targets it.

exercises.q: **Exercise 3.** Which files make up the current snapshot after v3?
exercises.code:
v0: ADD A   ADD B
v1: REMOVE A   ADD C
v2: ADD D
v3: REMOVE B
why: Ignores the REMOVE actions. That is the physical listing, not the snapshot.
That is the state after v2. v3 removed B.
exercises.explain: Replay the log: v0 → {A, B}. v1 removes A and adds C → {B, C}. v2 adds D → {B, C, D}. v3 removes B → **{C, D}**. A and B may still physically exist, but they are not logical members.

exercises.q: **Challenge Q1.** A folder containing `part-0000.parquet`, `part-0001.parquet` and `part-0002.parquet` automatically means you have a Delta table.
exercises.explain: False. Plain Parquet files do not imply a Delta transaction log. A Delta table is Parquet data files **plus** `_delta_log`, which records which files form each version.

exercises.q: **Challenge Q7.** What is the current snapshot?
exercises.code:
v0 ADD A
v0 ADD B
v1 REMOVE A
v1 ADD C
v2 ADD D
v3 REMOVE C
v3 ADD E
why: The physical files, ignoring every REMOVE.
exercises.explain: v0: {A, B}. v1: remove A, add C → {B, C}. v2: add D → {B, C, D}. v3: remove C, add E → **{B, D, E}**. If you forget a REMOVE, you get a superset that no version ever had.

exercises.q: Using the Q7 log (`v0 ADD A, ADD B · v1 REMOVE A, ADD C · v2 ADD D · v3 REMOVE C, ADD E`): **how many files** are in the current snapshot, and how many files were ever written in total? Enter only the **snapshot count**.
exercises.explain: 5 files were written (A–E), but the snapshot holds **3** (B, D, E). The difference (A and C) may still sit physically in storage. That is the gap between physical existence and logical membership.

exercises.q: **Challenge Q4.** A Parquet file physically exists in storage, but the current Delta snapshot no longer references it. It is still logically part of the current table.
exercises.explain: False. Logical membership is decided by the relevant table snapshot, not by whether a file physically exists. Removed files can linger until they are cleaned up, and they are still not part of the current table.

exercises.q: **Challenge Q10.** Which component primarily provides **transactional state**?
why: Grants are governance, not transaction state.
exercises.explain: The **Delta transaction log** records the ADD/REMOVE commits that define each version. Executors compute and Parquet stores rows. Unity Catalog grants control who may access data, not which files form a version.

exercises.q: **Challenge Q11.** Spark has physically written three replacement files, but the Delta transaction has not committed. A reader of the current table should already see those three files, because they physically exist.
exercises.explain: False. Physically creating files is not the same as publishing a committed table version. Until the commit lands in the log, readers keep seeing the previous snapshot. That is atomicity and isolation at work.

exercises.q: Order the snapshots produced by replaying the Exercise 3 log (`v0: ADD A, ADD B · v1: REMOVE A, ADD C · v2: ADD D · v3: REMOVE B`).
exercises.explain: Replay strictly in version order and apply each REMOVE and ADD. Every snapshot is a complete, valid state. Applying versions out of order produces a state the table never had.

exercises.q: A colleague replayed this log by hand. Click the line where the replay goes wrong.
exercises.fix:
v2 → {B, C, D}
v3 → {B, D, E}
exercises.explain: Log: `v0 ADD A, ADD B · v1 REMOVE A, ADD C · v2 ADD D · v3 REMOVE C, ADD E`. The error starts at `v2 → {A, B, C, D}`: v2 only adds D, so the state is {B, C, D}, because A was removed in v1. `v3 → {A, B, D, E}` carries the same mistake forward. The correct final snapshot is {B, D, E}.

exercises.q: Parquet data files or `_delta_log`? Sort each responsibility.

items.text: Knowing that B.parquet is no longer in the table

exercises.explain: Parquet files hold the **rows**, column-encoded and compressed. The `_delta_log` holds the **table state**: ADD/REMOVE actions and which files make up each version. That state is what makes snapshots and time travel possible.

exercises.q: Which later topics depend on understanding *physical existence ≠ logical membership*? (Select all.)
why: It reads old snapshots whose files may still exist.
It deletes files that are no longer referenced.
It is about columns, not file membership.
exercises.explain: DELETE, UPDATE and MERGE create replacement files and REMOVE old ones. Time Travel reads older snapshots. VACUUM physically cleans up files that are no longer referenced. Column pruning is a read optimization that does not depend on this idea.

exercises.q: You list `s3://shop/orders/` and see `X.parquet`, but `SELECT` on the Delta table never returns any of X's rows.

options.text: Whether the current snapshot (replayed from `_delta_log`) references X.parquet
options.fb: Right. Membership comes from the snapshot, not from the folder listing.

options.text: Increase the cluster size and rerun the query
options.fb: This isn't a capacity problem. More compute won't make an unreferenced file appear.

options.text: Re-read the folder with `spark.read.parquet(...)`
options.fb: That bypasses the log and would also return removed or uncommitted data. It hides the problem.

steps.prompt: The current snapshot does NOT reference X. Which explanation fits?

options.text: A later version REMOVEd X (e.g. after an UPDATE/DELETE), or X's transaction never committed
options.fb: Correct. Both leave a physical file that is not a logical member.

options.text: S3 is corrupting the file
options.fb: Storage is not the suspect. The file reads fine, it just isn't in the table.

options.text: Column pruning skipped the file
options.fb: Column pruning drops columns, not whole files.

options.text: X physically exists but is not logically part of the current table. That is expected behavior
options.fb: Yes: physical existence ≠ logical membership.

options.text: Manually add X to the folder again
options.fb: It's already in the folder. Only a commit makes a file part of the table.

options.text: Delete `_delta_log` so all files are read
options.fb: Never do this. You would destroy the table's state and expose stale files.

exercises.explain: Start from the log, not the folder listing. Check whether X is referenced by the current snapshot. If it isn't, find out why: a later REMOVE, a write that never committed, or a write that bypassed the log. Never point a plain Parquet reader at the folder to "fix" it.

exercises.q: Put the investigation for *"file exists in storage, rows not in the table"* in order.
items: Confirm the rows are missing when querying the table (not the folder)
Replay the log: is the file referenced by the current snapshot?
If not: was it REMOVEd by a later version, or never committed?
Check whether it was written by a plain Parquet write that bypassed the log
Conclude: physical existence ≠ logical membership, so fix the write path if needed
exercises.explain: Start by confirming the symptom from the table's point of view. Then consult the log for membership and explain the absence (REMOVE, missing commit, or a write that bypassed the log). Only then decide on a fix.

exercises.q: Order what happens (foundation model) when you run `DELETE FROM orders WHERE order_id = 123;`
exercises.explain: The engine finds the file holding the row, writes a replacement without it, and commits REMOVE old + ADD new as one transaction. Only after the commit does the snapshot point to the new file. Readers before the commit still see the old file.

exercises.q: **Challenge Q3.** Why can a Delta `DELETE` operation require creating new Parquet files?
options: Because Delta keeps every deleted row in a new 'trash' file
Because columnar files aren't edited cell by cell, so changes produce replacement files plus log metadata
Because Spark must convert Parquet to CSV before deleting
Because Unity Catalog requires a new file for every permission change
why: There's no 'trash file' in this model.
exercises.explain: Columnar data files are generally not edited as individual mutable cells. A change can mean writing replacement files, plus transaction metadata that marks which files now belong to the table. The other options describe things that aren't true.

exercises.q: Write the SQL to delete the e-shop order with id 123 from `orders`.
exercises.explain: This is ordinary DML syntax. On a Delta table it may turn into a file rewrite plus a REMOVE/ADD commit.

exercises.q: After `DELETE FROM orders WHERE order_id = 123` commits, `A.parquet` (the old file) has necessarily already been physically erased from storage.
exercises.explain: False. The commit removes A from the **current snapshot**, but the file can still physically exist for some time. Logical membership changed, and physical cleanup is a separate matter.

exercises.q: Click the wrong line(s) in this description of a DELETE.
exercises.fix:
write B.parquet containing 120,121,124,125
commit: ADD B.parquet
exercises.explain: "write B.parquet containing 120,121,123,…" is wrong: the replacement must not contain row 123, otherwise nothing is deleted. "commit: ADD A.parquet" is wrong: the commit must ADD the new file B. Re-adding A would leave row 123 in the table.

exercises.q: Foundation model: `A.parquet` holds **1,000,000** rows. `DELETE ... WHERE order_id = 123` matches exactly one row in A. How many rows must be written into the replacement file?
exercises.explain: The replacement holds every surviving row: 1,000,000 − 1 = **999,999**. Deleting one row can mean rewriting nearly a whole file, which is why later chapters cover optimizations for this.

exercises.q: Explain the difference between the *beginner model* and the *file-oriented model* of `DELETE` in 2–3 sentences.
exercises.model: The beginner imagines finding row 123 and erasing it in place. On file-oriented analytical storage, the engine instead writes a replacement file without the row and commits a transaction that REMOVEs the old file and ADDs the new one; the new snapshot points at the replacement.
exercises.explain: The key contrast is between **in-place row surgery** and **file replacement plus commit**. The table changes because the log now points to a different set of files.

exercises.q: Sort each trait by the **traditional** architecture it describes.

items.text: Historically rigid, separate from ML data

exercises.explain: Lakes were about **cheap, flexible, raw** storage that suits ML but had weak table guarantees. Warehouses were about **structured, transactional, governed** SQL/BI but were rigid and separate from raw/ML data. The lakehouse combines both.

exercises.q: Which best describes the **lakehouse** idea?
options: A warehouse that stores CSV exports
A lake with no schemas at all
Spark running inside a traditional database server
why: That's a raw lake without table semantics.
The lakehouse runs on object storage, not inside a DB server.
exercises.explain: A lakehouse combines **data-lake characteristics** (cheap object storage, files, flexible formats) with **database/warehouse semantics** (tables, transactions, governance). On Databricks, Delta Lake supplies much of the table side.

exercises.q: **Challenge Q13 (interview).** In one sentence, explain why *"Delta Lake is a database"* is an imprecise statement.
exercises.model: Delta Lake is a transactional storage/table layer over files (Parquet + a transaction log in object storage), not a standalone traditional database server.
exercises.explain: A strong answer says what Delta **is** (a table and transaction layer over files in storage) and what it **is not** (a standalone database server with its own engine). Compute comes from Spark/Photon, storage from cloud object storage and governance from Unity Catalog.

exercises.q: Databricks is essentially "Spark with notebooks".
exercises.explain: False. Databricks connects storage, transactional tables (Delta), Spark/Photon compute, governance (Unity Catalog), orchestration, SQL/BI, ML/AI and DevOps. Spark is only the compute part.

exercises.q: Which one is **not** a traditional data-lake characteristic?
exercises.explain: Cheap object storage, flexible formats and huge raw datasets describe the lake. Strong transactions with governed BI were the **warehouse's** strengths, and the lakehouse adds them to the lake.

exercises.q: Which statement about Delta Lake is the most precise?
options: A standalone database server that replaces Spark
The optimized storage/table layer underpinning lakehouse tables
The governance layer that grants permissions
why: It's not a server and doesn't replace Spark.
exercises.explain: Delta is the **optimized storage/table layer** that underpins lakehouse tables: Parquet plus a transaction log. It is not a server, not a compute engine and not the governance layer.

exercises.q: **Challenge Q8.** What does each part of `company.finance.transactions` represent in the Unity Catalog naming model?
exercises.explain: Unity Catalog names follow `catalog.schema.object`, so `company` is the catalog, `finance` is the schema and `transactions` is the object (table). The first part is **not** a server.

exercises.q: Metadata or data? Sort each item for the table `prod.sales.orders`.
exercises.explain: Metadata *describes* the table: names, columns and types, format, location, owner, permissions. Data is the rows themselves. Confusing the two is the root of the classic "Unity Catalog ≠ Delta" trap.

exercises.q: A colleague reads `ecommerce.silver.orders` as *server `ecommerce`, database `silver`, table `orders`*. What's wrong?
options: Nothing, that's exactly the UC model
`ecommerce` is a catalog, not a server: the model is catalog.schema.object
`silver` is the table and `orders` a column
UC uses only two levels: schema.table
exercises.explain: Unity Catalog uses `catalog.schema.object`, so `ecommerce` is a **catalog**. Mapping it to `server.database.table` from traditional databases is a common mental trap.

exercises.q: Fill the gaps.
exercises.text: Unity Catalog uses a [[three-level|3-level]] namespace: [[catalog]].[[schema]].[[object|table]]. In `ecommerce.silver.orders`, `silver` is the [[schema]].
exercises.explain: UC uses a **three-level** namespace: `catalog.schema.object`. Example: `ecommerce.silver.orders` → catalog `ecommerce`, schema `silver`, table `orders`.

exercises.q: Write a query that reads every column of the `orders` table in schema `silver` of catalog `ecommerce`.
exercises.explain: Use the full three-level name, `catalog.schema.table`, so there is no doubt about which object you mean.

exercises.q: Unity Catalog is where the actual rows of a table (e.g. `123, 4921, 79.95`) are stored.
exercises.explain: False. Unity Catalog is the **metadata and governance** layer: names, ownership and permissions. The rows live in Parquet data files (managed by Delta) in cloud storage.

exercises.q: Click the wrong line(s) in this metadata description of `prod.sales.orders`.
exercises.explain: "server: prod" is wrong: `prod` is the **catalog**. "database server: sales" is wrong: `sales` is the **schema**. The UC model is catalog.schema.object, not server.database.table.

exercises.q: **Challenge Q9.** Which component normally *executes* `df.groupBy("country").sum("amount")`?
why: Delta gives table semantics, not computation.
Parquet is just a file format.
exercises.explain: **Spark** is the compute engine that runs transformations and aggregations. Delta is the table format, Unity Catalog governs objects and Parquet is a file format. None of those execute anything.

exercises.q: **Challenge Q2.** What is the principal conceptual difference between **Spark** and **Delta Lake**?
exercises.model: Spark is primarily a distributed computation engine (it executes reads, transformations, joins, aggregations), while Delta Lake supplies transactional table/storage semantics (ACID, versions/snapshots via a transaction log) over data files in storage.
rubric: Delta works over data files (Parquet + log)
exercises.explain: Separate the *engine* from the *table layer*. Spark does the work in memory on executors. Delta defines what the table is: which Parquet files, which version, with ACID guarantees.

exercises.q: Order the layers of *the one diagram* from top (you) to bottom.
exercises.explain: You send SQL/Python to the **compute engine**, which reads and writes a **Delta table** (Parquet files + log), which physically lives in **cloud storage**. With `saveAsTable`, a Unity Catalog object sits on top of the Delta table as the governed name.

exercises.q: Write PySpark that saves DataFrame `df` as a **Delta** table at path `path` (path-based, not a catalog name).
exercises.explain: `format("delta")` makes Spark write Parquet data files **and** update the Delta transaction log. `df.write.parquet(path)` would write plain Parquet with no log.

exercises.q: Write PySpark that saves `df` as the governed table `orders` in schema `sales` of catalog `prod`.
exercises.explain: `saveAsTable` with a three-level name creates or updates a **Unity Catalog object** backed by a Delta table in cloud storage. That adds a governed layer on top of path-based writes.

exercises.q: Match each snippet to what it conceptually produces or does.
pairs: Writes Parquet files only, no transaction log
Writes Parquet files + updates Delta log at a path
Creates/updates a governed UC table backed by Delta
exercises.explain: `read.parquet` / `write.parquet` handle plain Parquet with no log. `format("delta").save` writes Parquet **plus** the Delta log at a path. `saveAsTable("catalog.schema.orders")` adds a governed UC object over the Delta table. Later chapters cover when these are equivalent and when they are not.

exercises.q: After `df.write.saveAsTable("prod.sales.orders")`, terminating the compute resource means `prod.sales.orders` necessarily disappears.
exercises.explain: False. Compute and persistent data have different lifetimes. The table's files and log live in cloud storage and its name lives in the catalog, so new compute can query it later.

exercises.q: Yesterday you ran `df.write.saveAsTable("prod.sales.orders")`, then terminated the cluster. Today a teammate says: *"The cluster is gone, so the table is gone, right?"*

options.text: No. Compute and persistent data have independent lifetimes, so the table should still exist
options.fb: Correct. Terminating compute removes RAM and temporary files, not the table in cloud storage.

options.text: Yes, we must rerun the whole pipeline
options.fb: That confuses compute with storage. The data was persisted.

options.text: It depends on whether the cluster had autoscaling
options.fb: Autoscaling changes compute size. It has nothing to do with table persistence.

steps.prompt: You start new compute, and the query still can't find the table. What do you check first?

options.text: That I'm using the exact full name `prod.sales.orders` (catalog.schema.table)
options.fb: Good. A wrong catalog or schema is a cheap, common cause.

options.text: Make the cluster bigger
options.fb: Size doesn't affect whether a name resolves.

options.text: Look for the old executors' shuffle files
options.fb: Those were temporary and are gone. They never held the table anyway.

steps.prompt: The name is correct, and still nothing. What next?

options.text: Check whether the original write actually ran and committed (vs. only building a DataFrame in memory)
options.fb: Right. If nothing was persisted or committed, there's nothing to find.

options.text: Conclude that Delta tables only live as long as the cluster
options.fb: False premise: Delta tables persist in cloud storage.

options.text: Read the driver's RAM dump
options.fb: The driver's memory is gone and never held the persisted table.

exercises.explain: Separate the lifetimes: compute is gone, but persistent data and catalog metadata are not. If the table really can't be found, look at the write (did it persist and commit?) and the name (full three-level name). Don't blame the terminated cluster.

exercises.q: Order the checks for *"my table seems gone after the cluster was terminated"*.
items: Remind myself: terminating compute doesn't delete persisted tables
Query the exact three-level name from new compute
Verify the write used saveAsTable / format("delta").save, not just an in-memory DataFrame
Verify the write committed a table version
Only then investigate storage / catalog configuration
exercises.explain: First fix the mental model (compute ≠ storage). Then check the cheap things: the exact name. Then the write itself: was it persisted and committed? Each step rules out a whole layer.

exercises.q: Control plane or compute plane?
exercises.explain: The **control plane** holds Databricks-managed services: the web app and coordination ("what should run?"). The **compute plane** is where data is actually processed ("actually run it"), whether serverless or classic.

exercises.q: For serverless workloads, compute runs in a Databricks-managed serverless compute plane. Classic compute uses cloud infrastructure associated with the customer's cloud environment.
exercises.explain: True. This is the source's first-preview distinction. Serverless means Databricks operates the compute. Classic means the compute runs in infrastructure tied to your own cloud environment.

exercises.q: Where does your workload *actually process data*?
why: The control plane decides and coordinates, but does not process your data.
exercises.explain: The **compute plane** is where data processing happens. The control plane coordinates and serves the web app. Unity Catalog and the Delta log are not planes: they are governance and table-state layers.

exercises.q: A team uses **classic** compute. Whose cloud environment hosts the compute infrastructure?
why: The control plane hosts platform services, not your classic clusters.
The metastore is metadata, not compute.
exercises.explain: Classic compute uses cloud infrastructure associated with the **customer's** cloud environment. It's the serverless case where Databricks operates the compute plane, so mixing the two up is a typical trap.

exercises.q: Which one doesn't belong with the **control plane**?
exercises.explain: The web application, coordination and "what should run?" all describe the control plane. Processing data on executors happens in the **compute plane**.

exercises.q: `spark.read.table("sales.orders").groupBy("country").sum("amount").show()` is extremely slow. Walk through it like a professional.

options.text: Identify which layer could be responsible (storage, layout, Delta, Spark, data, compute, query, stats, network)
options.fb: Yes. Finding the layer comes before any fix.

options.text: Increase the cluster size
options.fb: That's the anti-pattern: a fix without a diagnosis.

options.text: Blame Spark and rewrite in pandas
options.fb: "Spark" is not a diagnosis, and this throws away distributed compute.

steps.prompt: You suspect the table layout. What do you do next?

options.text: Collect evidence, e.g. check whether the scan reads a huge number of tiny files
options.fb: Right. Get evidence for or against the hypothesis.

options.text: Immediately rewrite the whole table
options.fb: That's a fix before any evidence. You might rewrite for nothing.

options.text: Add more executors
options.fb: That doesn't test the hypothesis.

steps.prompt: You applied a fix. What's the last step?

options.text: Remeasure and compare with the original symptom
options.fb: Correct. A fix isn't done until it has been measured.

options.text: Assume it worked and move on
options.fb: Unverified fixes are guesses.

options.text: Scale the cluster too, just in case
options.fb: Then you can't tell which change helped.

exercises.explain: Professionals go symptom → layer → evidence → hypothesis → metrics → fix → remeasure. Scaling the cluster blindly may hide the problem, cost more, or change nothing if the cause is in storage, layout, skew or statistics.

exercises.q: Put the professional debugging loop in order.
exercises.explain: Symptom → identify layer → collect evidence → form hypothesis → check Spark/Databricks metrics → fix → remeasure. Skipping to "increase cluster size" jumps straight from symptom to an untested fix.

exercises.q: Match each layer to the hypothesis you'd test for a slow query.
exercises.explain: Each layer has its own typical failure. Storage gives slow reads, table layout gives many tiny files, data gives skew, statistics give bad optimizer choices, and network gives huge exchanges. Naming the layer tells you what evidence to collect.

exercises.q: A query is slow. Which response best shows **professional** Databricks operation?
options: Increase the cluster size right away
Identify the layer, collect evidence, form a hypothesis, check metrics, fix, remeasure
Restart the cluster until it's fast
why: That makes everything worse: no columnar pruning.
exercises.explain: The professional identifies the layer and gathers evidence before fixing. "Increase cluster size" may hide the real cause (tiny files, skew, bad statistics) while costing more.

exercises.q: Round-1 review: sort the statements.

items.text: Delta = Parquet data files + transaction log
Unity Catalog governs objects; Delta is the table format
Storage and compute have independent lifetimes
If a file exists in the table folder, it's in the current table
Metadata and data are the same thing
A table is just its storage directory

exercises.explain: Each true line keeps two layers apart. Each false line merges layers that are only related. The exam often hides exactly these confusions inside longer answer options.

exercises.q: Click the wrong statements in this Round-1 cheat sheet.
exercises.fix:
Delta ≠ Parquet (Parquet + transaction log)
physical file existence ≠ current table membership
Unity Catalog ≠ Delta Lake
exercises.explain: "Delta = Parquet" is wrong: Delta adds a transaction log to Parquet. "file exists ⇒ in current table" is wrong: physical existence ≠ current membership. "Unity Catalog = Delta Lake" is wrong: UC is governance and metadata, Delta is the table format.

exercises.q: Three of these are *layers* to suspect for a slow query. Which one is **not** a layer but an anti-pattern fix?
exercises.explain: Storage, table layout and statistics are layers you investigate. "Increase cluster size" is a fix applied without evidence: the anti-pattern this section warns about.

exercises.q: Interview: *"Our `groupBy("country").sum("amount")` on `sales.orders` is slow. What do you do?"* Answer in 3–5 sentences.
exercises.model: I wouldn't start by scaling the cluster. I'd first identify the layer: storage (slow reads), table layout (many tiny files), Delta organization, Spark (huge shuffle), data (skewed country), compute (insufficient resources), query, statistics (bad optimizer choice) or network (huge exchange). Then I'd collect evidence — Spark UI/metrics, the plan — form a hypothesis, apply a targeted fix, and remeasure against the original symptom.
exercises.explain: A strong answer names several layers, says how you would get **evidence** for each, and closes with remeasurement. It also explicitly rejects "just scale the cluster".
